Package org.aeonbits.owner.loaders

Class SourceOptions

java.lang.Object
org.aeonbits.owner.loaders.SourceOptions
public final class SourceOptions extends Object
The options written on a single source, and the one place every Loader reads them from.

The rule is the same for every loader and every scheme: the query belongs to the protocol and the fragment belongs to OWNER. 

     @Sources("file:.env#dialect=dotenv&quotes=strip")
     @Sources("https://config/app.env?token=abc#dialect=dotenv")

The second line is why it is the fragment rather than the query. A query means something to the server that answers an http: source, so a loader cannot claim it without breaking that source; a fragment is never sent to a server at all. It also survives where a query does not: a resource inside a jar resolves to an opaque URI such as jar:file:/a.jar!/app.env, where URI.getQuery() returns null while the fragment is still read.

The practical consequence is that a loader has nothing to strip. URL.getFile() excludes the fragment, so both accept and openStream() see the plain resource, and the options are read beside them rather than cut out of them.

An option that is not recognised is refused, never ignored - see refuseUnknown(String...). A misspelt option that passes in silence is a configuration that is wrong and says nothing, which is the failure this class exists to prevent.

2.0.0

  • Field Details

    • REQUIRED

      public static final String REQUIRED
      The option that says a source has to be there, read by the library rather than by a loader.

      It is the one name every loader accepts without declaring it, and that is the whole difference between the two kinds of option in a fragment. A dialect or a validation flag is a way of reading that format and belongs to the loader that understands it; whether a source is allowed to be missing is decided before any loader is chosen, and is the same question for all of them. A loader refusing it as unknown is what would happen otherwise, which is why it is here and not there.

      See Also:
      • Constant Field Values

  • Method Details

    • path

      public static String path(URI uri)
      The part of a source to match an extension against: no query, no fragment, and no assumption that the URI is hierarchical.

      URI.getPath() cannot be used for this. file:.env - the form the documentation uses, since the path is relative - is an opaque URI whose path is null, and so is every resource resolved inside a jar. The text is what both have in common.

      Parameters:
      uri - the source, may be null.
      Returns:
      the source without its query or fragment; an empty string when the URI is null.

    • hasExtension

      public static boolean hasExtension(URI uri, String... extensions)
      Whether a source ends in one of the given extensions, which is what most Loader.accept(URI) implementations amount to.

      Built on path(URI), so it is not fooled by a query, by the options in the fragment, or by an opaque URI - the three things a hand-written endsWith gets wrong, and did. The comparison ignores case, because a file called CONFIG.XML is an XML file.

      A loader keeps the list in one constant and uses it here and in Loader.defaultSpecsFor(String), so that the names a format goes by are written once.

      Parameters:
      uri - the source, may be null.
      extensions - the extensions to match, dot included.
      Returns:
      whether the source ends in one of them.

    • of

      public static SourceOptions of(URI uri)
      Reads the options written on a source.
      Parameters:
      uri - the source, may be null.
      Returns:
      the options, in the order they were written; never null.
      Throws:
      UnsupportedOperationException - if the fragment holds something that is not a list of name=setting pairs, or if the source carries a query on a scheme where a query cannot mean anything. Unchecked on purpose: an IOException here would be caught by Config.LoadType and the source dropped in silence.

    • refuseUnknown

      public void refuseUnknown(String... known)
      Refuses every option whose name is not in the given list.

      The message names the offending option, the source it was written on, and the options that would have been accepted. That last part is not politeness: the day a loader starts refusing, the people it refuses first are the ones whose configuration was already wrong and silently doing nothing, and they need to be told what to write instead rather than only what not to.

      Parameters:
      known - the option names this loader understands; none at all means the loader takes no options.
      Throws:
      UnsupportedOperationException - if any option is not among them.

      Throws:
